title: J.P. Morgan Pulls Fed Rate Hike Call Forward to December After July Hold
excerpt: The investment bank now expects a quarter-point rate increase in December, accelerating its previous forecast for a hike in the second half of 2027, after the Fed kept rates unchanged amid persistent inflation.
body:
• J.P. Morgan now expects a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike in December 2026, brought forward from a previous forecast of a hike in the second half of 2027.
  • The Fed held rates steady at 3.75%-4.00% at its July meeting, with three of 12 FOMC members dissenting in favor of an increase.
  • Markets are pricing in a 65.2% chance of a September rate hike, down from 81% before the policy statement.
  • Other major banks remain split: Goldman Sachs and Barclays expect no hike this year, while BofA forecasts three increases starting in September.

J.P. Morgan Shifts Timeline on Fed Tightening

J.P. Morgan has moved up its forecast for the next Federal Reserve rate hike to December 2026, abandoning its prior call for an increase sometime in the second half of 2027. The shift came after the Fed's July meeting, where policymakers voted to keep the federal funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%.

The bank said in a note Wednesday that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's remarks at the meeting raised doubts about the new chair's credibility in delivering lower inflation, which could increase the urgency for the rest of the Federal Open Market Committee to act.

"Warsh's remarks cast doubt on the new chair's credibility in delivering lower inflation, which could increase the urgency for the rest of the committee to act on its mandate."

— J.P. Morgan, research note

Three Dissenters Push for Immediate Action

The widely anticipated decision to hold rates drew an unusually strong dissent from three of the FOMC's 12 voting members, all of whom favored a quarter-percentage-point increase. That level of opposition signals growing tension within the committee over whether the Fed is moving too slowly to address inflation that has remained above its 2% target for more than five years.

Underlying price pressures have been accelerating in recent months, driven by higher fuel and food costs along with strong business spending tied to the artificial intelligence boom. Despite those pressures, Warsh did not frame a rate hike as necessarily the right response.

Wall Street Consensus Fractures

The call puts J.P. Morgan in the hawkish camp on Wall Street, where opinions on the Fed's next move are increasingly divided. Goldman Sachs and Barclays both continue to expect the central bank to keep rates unchanged through year-end. BofA Global Research takes the most aggressive stance, forecasting three rate hikes starting as early as September.

On the dovish end, Citigroup maintained its forecast for rate cuts in October and December 2026 and another in January 2027, sticking with a view that the economy will slow enough to justify easing.

Markets have recalibrated as well. The CME Group's FedWatch tool shows traders pricing in a 65.2% probability of a September rate hike, down sharply from 81% before the July policy statement was released.

What It Means for Markets

J.P. Morgan expects the Fed to hold rates at 3.75%-4.00% after a December hike, while cautioning that a September increase remains possible if inflation data continues to run hot. The bank's economists see the risk of an earlier move as a live possibility rather than a base case.

The divergence among major banks reflects genuine uncertainty about where the economy is heading. Inflation has proven stickier than most forecasters expected, but some economic indicators — particularly in the labor market — have shown signs of cooling that could give the Fed cover to stay on hold.

For investors and borrowers alike, the lack of consensus means volatility is likely to remain elevated around upcoming inflation reports and Fed meetings.
